```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
# The article downloads its prices from Yahoo Finance while it is built. The downloads are
# made here first, out of sight, so the chunks below get them from the disk cache, and
# without them the code is shown without its results instead of failing the build.
online <- tryCatch(
  {
    spx <- golemstockindices::get_history("S&P 500", as.Date("1990-01-01"))
    three <- golemstockindices::get_history(c("S&P 500", "Euro Stoxx 50", "Nikkei 225"))
    !is.null(spx) && !is.null(three) && length(unique(three$label)) == 3
  },
  error = function(e) FALSE
)
# The exchange rates come from Yahoo Finance too, but from another request.
rates <- online && tryCatch(
  !is.null(golemstockindices::convert_prices(golemstockindices::get_history("DAX"), "USD")),
  error = function(e) FALSE
)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = online)
```

`r if (!online) "> The prices could not be downloaded when this page was built, so the code is shown without its results."`

The charts of the [golemstockindices app](https://sedzinfo-golemstockindices.share.connect.posit.cloud/) are also R functions. Each one takes the prices you download with `get_history()` and returns an interactive [plotly](https://plotly.com/r/) chart. Run it in the console and the chart opens in the RStudio Viewer or your browser. In an R Markdown or Quarto document it appears in the page.

This article shows the price charts. [Volatility, drawdowns and seasonality](analyses.html) shows the charts of the analyses, and [The market overview](market.html) shows the table and the chart that put all the indices side by side.

## Install and load the package

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("golemstockindices",
  repos = c("https://sedzinfo.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
```

```{r library}
library(golemstockindices)
```

The prices need no API key. They come from Yahoo Finance.

## Find an index

Indices are picked by their label, such as `"S&P 500"`. `get_indices()` lists them, with the `label` of each, its `region`, the `currency` of the shares in it and its `type`:

```{r indices}
indices <- get_indices()
table(indices$region)
head(indices[, c("label", "region", "currency", "type")])
```

The `type` is `"price"` for an index that leaves out the dividends of its companies, such as the S&P 500, and `"total return"` for one that reinvests them, such as the DAX. The charts mark the total return indices (TR). The VIX measures the expected volatility of the S&P 500, so it has no currency and no type.

## Download the prices

`get_history()` downloads the daily prices of one or more indices from a start date on, a year ago by default. They are in index points, and there is a row per day on which the exchange traded:

```{r history}
spx <- get_history("S&P 500", as.Date("1990-01-01"))
tail(spx[, c("label", "timestamp", "open", "high", "low", "close", "volume")])
```

Each index's prices are kept on disk between R sessions. Once they are more than an hour old, only the last two weeks are downloaded again, so later calls are fast. The history of the S&P 500 goes back to 1927. This article starts at 1990, to keep the page light.

## Candlestick chart

`plot_timeseries()` draws the daily open, high, low and close prices of one index as candles, with a line through the close and its 50- and 200-day moving averages. The smaller charts underneath show the trading volume and the drawdown: how far the price is below its all-time high so far.

```{r timeseries, fig.height = 9}
plot_timeseries(spx)
```

Zoom with the range buttons (1 year, 6 months, 7 days, ...) or the slider under the chart. The Linear and Log buttons switch the axis of the prices, and a click on a legend entry hides or shows that line.

The averages and the drawdown are calculated over the history you pass. Pass all of it and zoom on the chart, rather than downloading a shorter history. A history that starts in 1990 has no 200-day average before its 200th day, and its drawdown is measured from the highest close since 1990.

Choose other moving averages with `averages`, or none with `averages = NULL`. Leave out the drawdown chart with `show_drawdown = FALSE`. A chart of a long history is large, so this one is not drawn here, to keep the page light:

```{r timeseries-options, eval = FALSE}
plot_timeseries(spx, averages = c(20, 100), show_drawdown = FALSE)
```

## Compare indices

To compare several indices, download them together and pass them through `normalize_prices()`. It starts every index at 100 on the first date on which all of them have data, so 150 means the price rose by half since that date:

```{r compare, fig.height = 7}
history <- get_history(c("S&P 500", "Euro Stoxx 50", "Nikkei 225"))
prices <- normalize_prices(history)
tail(prices[, c("label", "timestamp", "close", "index")])
plot_compare(prices)
```

The Linear and Log buttons switch the vertical axis. On the log axis equal distances are equal percentages. The history is the last year, because that is what `get_history()` downloads when it has no start date.

## Currency conversion

Each index is in the money of its shares, so a chart of indices from several countries mixes currencies. `convert_prices()` converts the prices to US dollars (`"USD"`) or euros (`"EUR"`); `"local"`, the default, leaves them as they are. It multiplies each price by the exchange rate of its day, from Yahoo Finance. Volumes and the VIX are left as they are.

Pass the converted history to `normalize_prices()` and tell `plot_compare()` the currency, for the title:

```{r euros, eval = rates, fig.height = 7}
euros <- convert_prices(history, "EUR")
plot_compare(normalize_prices(euros), currency = "EUR")
```

`r if (online && !rates) "> The exchange rates could not be downloaded when this page was built, so the chart above is not drawn."`

The daily rates are not taken at the close of each exchange, so the change of a single day mixes in a few hours of the moves of the currency. Over weeks and months this matters little.

## Monthly returns

`monthly_returns()` turns an index's prices into a matrix of returns in percent, with a row per year and a column per month. `plot_returns_calendar()` draws it as a heatmap, from red for falls to green for rises:

```{r calendar, fig.height = 7}
returns <- monthly_returns(spx)
tail(returns, 3)
plot_returns_calendar(returns, "S&P 500")
```

Each month's return is its last close relative to the last close of the month before. The first month and the months still to come are empty.

## Dark mode

Every chart function has a `mode` argument. `mode = "dark"` uses light text and grid lines on a transparent background, for a page with a dark background. On this page, which is light, its text would not show, so the code is not run here:

```{r dark, eval = FALSE}
plot_timeseries(spx, mode = "dark")
```

## Save or change a chart

The charts are plotly objects, so the functions of the plotly and htmlwidgets packages work on them. To save a chart as a web page that opens in any browser:

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
chart <- plot_compare(prices)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(chart, "compare.html")
```

To change the layout, for example to add a title:

```{r layout, eval = FALSE}
plotly::layout(chart,
  title = "The S&P 500, the Euro Stoxx 50 and the Nikkei 225 over the last year")
```
